Volume 13 · Chapter 12

Theory synthesis and research critique

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c11

By the endEvaluate a theoretical contribution through proofs, counterexamples and economic relevance.

Volume 13 · Chapter 12

Theory synthesis and research critique

A theory paper can contain correct algebra and still make an unsupported economic claim. Its optimizer may be only local. Its equilibrium may be one of several. Its welfare comparison may depend on an unstated interpersonal scale. Its fitted model may share every observed prediction with a model that recommends a different policy. A useful referee must identify the exact gap, show why it matters and distinguish a repair of the proof from a change in the model.

Capability. Evaluate a theoretical contribution through its question, primitives, quantifiers, proof dependencies, counterexamples and economic interpretation. Six fully worked cases develop complete global arguments and a substantive benchmark referee report. Twelve transfer exercises require determinate solutions or an evidence-based critique; they assess reasoning rather than conformity to a policy view.

Prerequisites. Preferences and choice separates preferences from their representations. Consumer and producer theory develops optimization; General equilibrium supplies existence-proof discipline. Static games and refinements supplies mixed best replies and recommendation-dependent obedience. Information economics and screening, Contracts and dynamic incentives and Mechanism design and auctions distinguish information, commitment, participation and implementation. Matching, networks and market design supplies finite strict matching terminology. The matching transfer below checks its own seven possibilities; it assumes no group-incentive, ties or couples theorem. Volume 2 supplies calculus, compactness and contraction arguments.

Every economy, payoff, numerical bound and submitted claim in this chapter is an original instructional construction. The fictional report is not a review of an actual submission. Mathematical verification and an internal rubric do not certify a learner’s research originality, publication quality or professional judgment; those require external human evaluation and experience.

1. Identify the claim before checking its proof

Begin with a precise question: whose choice or welfare is at issue, relative to which alternative, and under which information and institutional constraints? A primitive is part of the model: a feasible set, preference, technology, information structure, timing or enforceable right. A solution concept specifies which outcomes count as solutions. A selection rule chooses among several solutions. An interpretation connects these mathematical objects to an economic setting. An empirical restriction says which possible observations a model permits. These roles can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

Consider five sentences. “An equilibrium is a fixed point of this response map” is a definition, until the response map is given economic content. “There exists a fixed point” is an existence assertion. “Every equilibrium is efficient” is a conditional theorem with a universal quantifier. “The economy moves to this equilibrium after a grant” is a selection or adjustment claim requiring its own argument. “A grant caused observed adoption to rise” is an empirical causal claim, requiring evidence and identifying conditions beyond a solved model. The existence proof does not establish the last three sentences.

For each important claim, keep a compact ledger: the question; the primitives and domain; the conclusion and its quantifiers; the tools actually needed; a proof or an explicit counterexample; and the interpretation that survives. “For every parameter there exists an equilibrium” does not mean that one equilibrium works for every parameter. A property of one selected equilibrium is not a property of all equilibria. An almost-everywhere statement does not automatically cover a boundary type. A numerical check on finitely many inputs cannot prove a claim over a continuum unless a separate argument reduces that continuum to the checked cases.

There are several possible repairs. A missing argument can sometimes be supplied without changing the result. A false universal claim can be narrowed to the domain on which the proof works. A counterexample can motivate an explicitly altered primitive or a new question. These have different implications for a paper’s contribution. Do not present a changed payoff, tie convention or feasible set as if it had always been part of the original theorem.

Method route: Board and Meyer-ter-Vehn, Writing Economic Theory Papers, October 2018, pages 1–7, motivates a clear economic question, explicit primitives and a separation of result, proof and intuition. The claim ledger and all models below are original constructions; this guidance is not evidence that a particular interpretation is empirically correct.

2. A well-defined optimum can rest on an unstated welfare choice

Worked case 1. Rescaling one person’s utility reverses the chosen allocation

Two people share a divisible resource of size 12. Feasible allocations satisfy x,y≥0 and x+y≤12. Own utility representations are u1(x)=log(1+x) and u2(y)=log(1+y). There is no numeraire or interpersonal utility scale in these primitives. A proposed theorem says that the unique maximizer of u1+u2 is a social-welfare conclusion implied by the two preferences alone.

Conditional optimization. Both utilities are strictly increasing, so any sum maximizer uses the entire resource. Put y=12−x. The derivative of log(1+x)+log(13−x) is 1/(1+x)−1/(13−x); it vanishes at x=6. The second derivative is strictly negative on [0,12], so the unique global sum maximizer is (6,6). This is a valid result conditional on that particular objective.

Now replace only u1 by 4u1. Every comparison of person 1’s feasible bundles is unchanged. Positive affine rescaling also preserves that person’s expected-utility comparisons when such a representation is used; this is not an appeal to arbitrary nonlinear transformation of risky utility. Yet the derivative of 4log(1+x)+log(13−x) vanishes where 4(13−x)=1+x. Strict concavity gives the different unique global sum optimum (51/5,9/5). The same individual preferences therefore do not identify the unweighted interpersonal sum.

Complete weight sensitivity. For λ∈[0,1], consider Wλ(x)=λlog(1+x)+(1−λ)log(13−x). Its derivative has the sign of 14λ−1−x, since its denominator (1+x)(13−x) is positive. Therefore

x*(λ)=min{12,max{0,14λ−1}},   y*(λ)=12−x*(λ).

For 0<λ<1 the objective is strictly concave, so the derivative sign proves the unique interior or boundary optimum. At λ=0 or 1, strict monotonicity selects the corresponding endpoint. The transition weights are (1/14,13/14), and interior allocation sensitivity is 14. The rescaled sum is equivalent to λ=4/5 after multiplying the whole objective by a positive constant.

Pareto frontier, proved separately. Every slack allocation can increase someone’s resource without reducing the other’s, so it is not Pareto efficient. At any full-use allocation, increasing one person’s utility requires increasing that person’s quantity. Feasibility then reduces the other’s quantity and utility. Thus every allocation on x+y=12 is Pareto efficient. Pareto efficiency does not choose among the two sum optima—or among any of the other full-use allocations.

Referee judgment. The optimization theorem is correct; the claim that its welfare criterion follows from preferences alone is not. A repair must state welfare weights or an economically justified common money-metric normalization as additional structure. Observing the agents’ choices under unchanged feasible sets cannot select between positive rescalings that preserve all those choices. The sensitivity in λ is a change in a normative weight, not a behavioral parameter estimated by the calculation.

3. Certify the global claim and the approximation it actually uses

Worked case 2. A strict local maximum loses twenty-seven units

A planner chooses capacity x∈[0,5]. Its stipulated net real benefit is the polynomial with ascending nonconstant coefficients (96,−84,28,−3):

V(x)=−3x⁴+28x³−84x²+96x.

A solver reports x=1 and a zero gradient with negative second derivative. The submitted argument calls this the globally optimal policy. First check existence: V is continuous on the compact nonempty interval, so a maximum is attained. This does not identify the maximum.

Complete global calculation. The derivative factors as V′(x)=−12(x−1)(x−2)(x−4). Its signs on (0,1),(1,2),(2,4),(4,5) are respectively +,−,+,−. The critical points are (1,2,4), and their second derivatives are (−36,24,−72). Every possible maximum is among the endpoints and critical points. Values at x=0,1,2,4,5 are (0,37,32,64,5). Hence x=4 is the unique global maximizer, with value sixty-four. The solver’s strict local maximum at one has exact regret 27. A zero gradient does not even distinguish it from the stationary local minimum at two without a curvature check; adding that check still does not resolve the global comparison.

One repair is to supply the missing sign and value comparison for this original objective. Another is to state a different model class with a valid concavity hypothesis. For example, Q(x)=64−3(x−4)² on [0,5] is globally strictly concave and has unique optimum four. At candidate 23/6, Q′=1 and the exact loss is 1/12. Completing the square proves the loss calculation. This changed objective illustrates a useful sufficient structure; it does not make the original quartic concave.

A sharp approximation theorem. Let f be continuous on a compact nonempty K. Suppose a computed objective f̂ has uniform error supK|f−f̂|≤ε, and a returned x̂∈K has a global objective certificate supKf̂−f̂(x̂)≤η, where ε,η≥0. Then

maxKf−f(x̂)≤2ε+η.

Proof. Take an attained true maximizer x*. Insert and subtract f̂ at x* and x̂:

f(x*)−f(x̂)=[f(x*)−f̂(x*)]+[f̂(x*)−f̂(x̂)]+[f̂(x̂)−f(x̂)]≤ε+η+ε.

No maximizer of f̂ is required beyond the supplied approximate-supremum certificate. That certificate cannot be replaced by stationarity or a small gradient: the quartic gives a zero-gradient point with positive regret. Exercise 4 proves that the bound is sharp. A referee should request the relevant global certificate or narrow the claim, rather than request an unspecified larger collection of solver runs.

4. Solve the equilibrium correspondence before interpreting a policy

Worked case 3. Subsidizing adoption lowers an interior mixed branch

Two simultaneous agents choose ai∈{0,1}. Adoption costs one in real resources and yields benefit three if the other agent adopts. The common grant is s∈[0,3/2]; utility is ai(3aj−1+s). The benefit and action cost are (3,1). Each agent can cover its own cost. Before actions, a separate sponsor commits actual cash 2s, pays s to each adopter afterward and retains unused cash. Transfers are enforceable and create no resources. The sponsor has no direct adoption benefit. Mixed Nash actions are independently randomized; pi denotes i’s adoption probability.

The expected gain from adopting instead of not adopting is 3pj−1+s. The best reply is adoption if this is positive, nonadoption if it is negative, and any mixture if it is zero. This gives the complete equilibrium set, not just favorable candidates.

For 0≤s<1, both (p1,p2)=(0,0) and (1,1) are equilibria. If one player is pure, the other’s strict best reply forces the same pure coordination outcome, so no one-sided mixture is possible. If both mix, both gain equations must vanish, giving p1=p2=(1−s)/3. This exhausts all supports. At s=1, the gain is 3pj. Any positive probability by one player forces the other to adopt with certainty, which then forces the first to adopt with certainty. Thus only (0,0) and (1,1) remain; weak equality at zero does not eliminate no adoption. For s>1, adoption is strictly dominant for each agent, and (1,1) is the unique equilibrium, including among mixed profiles.

Policy comparison and accounts. At s=0, the interior probabilities are (1/3,1/3). At the funded subsidy 1/2, they become (1/6,1/6). Each mixing agent has expected utility zero because its two pure actions tie. Sponsor expected spending is s(p1+p2). Adding agent utilities and the sponsor’s wealth change cancels grants, giving expected real welfare

W(p)=6p1p2−p1−p2.

The independent mixed branch has welfare zero without a subsidy and −1/6 at s=1/2, when expected sponsor spending is 1/6. By contrast, full adoption at that subsidy gives total agent utility, sponsor loss and real welfare (5,1,4). No adoption gives zero in every account. A sponsor with the committed cash one can pay in every realization, not merely on average.

Interpretation. The interior branch’s probability falls with s because an agent needs a lower chance of the other adopting to remain indifferent. This does not say that a real population must choose that branch. The pure branches persist until the strict-dominance threshold. Existence alone supplies neither a unique policy prediction nor a convergence mechanism. A claim about every equilibrium must survive all branches; a claim about one selected branch must state why that selection is appropriate. Exercise 6 changes the joint recommendation law while holding marginals fixed and shows why independent mixing and correlation are different incentive problems.

Formal background: Yildiz, Graduate Game Theory, Spring 2022 notes, printed pages 36–39 and 46–48, supplies finite mixed Nash and correlated-equilibrium definitions already inspected for Chapter 6. Every equilibrium, boundary and obedience comparison here is derived from the new payoff primitives; no general selection or learning theorem is imported.

5. A fixed point, a convergent algorithm and an accurate model are distinct

Worked case 4. Certifying an activity-adjustment model

Suppose standardized activity follows the stipulated deterministic adjustment law xt+1=Tθ(xt)=(θ+xt²)/4, with x∈[0,1] and θ∈[0,3]. A stationary equilibrium means a fixed point of this law. We are not claiming an optimizing-agent microfoundation that has not been supplied. The baseline parameter is 7/4.

Invariant domain and contraction. For every permitted x and θ, 0≤Tθ(x)≤(θ+1)/4≤1, so iteration never leaves the declared domain. For any x,y in it,

|Tθ(x)−Tθ(y)|=|x−y|(x+y)/4≤|x−y|/2.

Existence and convergence, proved. Starting anywhere in [0,1], repeated application gives |xt+1−xt|≤2−t|x1−x0|. For m>n, summing these increments gives |xm−xn|≤21−n|x1−x0|. The sequence is Cauchy and has a limit in the closed interval. Continuity then gives x*=Tθ(x*). Uniqueness. Two fixed points would have distance at most half their own distance, hence distance zero. Every starting point therefore converges to the same fixed point. Domain invariance, existence, uniqueness and convergence each have an explicit step; they are not interchangeable solver messages.

The fixed-point equation has roots 2±√(4−θ). Only the minus root lies in [0,1] for θ∈[0,3]; the other lies in [3,4]. At the baseline, the admissible root and other algebraic root are (1/2,7/2). From x0=0 the first two iterates are (7/16,497/1024).

Residual certificate. For any candidate x̂ in [0,1], insert Tθ(x̂) between x̂ and the true fixed point. The triangle and contraction inequalities give |x̂−x*|≤|x̂−Tθ(x̂)|+(1/2)|x̂−x*|. Thus the true distance is at most twice the true residual. For candidate 3/5, residual, certified bound and actual distance are (29/400,29/200,1/10). The bound is conservative but proved; a residual alone would be uninterpretable without the stability constant.

Parameter sensitivity. Comparing fixed points for θ and θ′, use the same contraction inequality and supx|Tθ(x)−Tθ′(x)|=|θ−θ′|/4. Rearranging gives |x*(θ)−x*(θ′)|≤|θ−θ′|/2. The changed parameter 51/25 has exact fixed point 3/5. Parameter difference and the output-to-parameter secant ratio are (29/100,10/29). Differentiating the explicit interior root gives dx*/dθ=1/(4−2x*), equal to 1/3 at the baseline. A local derivative is not the uniform one-half bound.

Separate numerical and model error. Suppose a computed map T̂ has uniform error at most ε against the stated Tθ, and a returned point has computed residual |x̂−T̂(x̂)|≤η. The triangle inequality first bounds the true residual by ε+η, then the previous certificate gives |x̂−x*|≤2(ε+η). This conclusion is conditional on those two justified bounds; it asserts neither that T̂ is a contraction nor that T̂ has a fixed point.

At x̂=3/5 under the baseline, simultaneous claims ε=η=1/100 cannot hold: their combined residual bound is 1/50, below the actual 29/400. They would also give a distance bound 1/25, below the actual 1/10. If uniform model error truly is 1/100, numerical residual must be at least 1/16. There is a valid different explanation: the map with θ=51/25 fixes 3/5 exactly, but differs uniformly from the original by 29/400. That is a solved changed model, not an accurate solution of the baseline model.

6. Exact observational fit does not choose a counterfactual model

Worked case 5. Two markets with the same observed law and different tax effects

The observed state Z is −1 or 1, each with probability one half. A competitive price-taking producer supplies a good at real numeraire cost C(q)=q²/4. Its profit psq−C(q) is strictly concave and gives the unconstrained supply q=2ps at nonnegative seller prices. Consider two possible price-taking buyer models:

BA(q,Z)=(4+2Z)q−q²/4,   DA(pb,Z)=8−2pb+4Z;
BB(q,Z)=(3+3Z/2)q−q²/8,   DB(pb,Z)=12−4pb+6Z.

These are unconstrained demand expressions when positive; without a cash constraint, the strictly concave buyer problem gives their positive parts. The demand slopes are (2,4). The buyer has initial cash twenty and the producer initial working resources ten. A unit tax τ∈[0,1] creates the wedge pb=ps+τ; the seller receives buyer spending, retains psq and remits τq to a government account initially zero. Real production consumes C(q) units of numeraire. Trading, delivery and tax remittance are enforceable. No borrowing or uncertain credit receipt finances production. At a seller price ps≥0, the actual prefunded supply is min{2ps,√40}. At a positive buyer price pb, actual demand in either model is min{max{0,Dunconstrained},20/pb}; at pb=0 it is the unconstrained nonnegative demand. These cash-limited responses, with pb=ps+τ, define the market at off-equilibrium prices as well. The declared buyer/producer initial funds are (20,10).

The entire no-tax observation law. Clearing demand against q=2ps at τ=0 gives pb=ps=2+Z and q=4+2Z in both models. The two equally likely observed (Z,p,q) states are ((−1,1,2),(1,3,6)). Thus the full joint distribution of these observations is identical, not just selected moments or a fitted line. Neither exact fit nor more repetitions from this same two-state law distinguish the models.

Maintained structural intervention. Hold each model’s benefit and cost equations fixed and impose the tax. Clearing gives

A:   ps=2+Z−τ/2,   q=4+2Z−τ,   pb=2+Z+τ/2;
B:   ps=2+Z−2τ/3,   q=4+2Z−4τ/3,   pb=2+Z+τ/3.

For every Z∈{−1,1}, τ∈[0,1], these prices and quantities are positive. Cash-limited demand is strictly decreasing wherever positive: both the unconstrained positive-demand branch and the positive cash-cap branch decrease strictly, and taking their minimum preserves this property. Actual supply is nondecreasing and may plateau at its cash cap. Demand is positive at ps=0 for every stated Z and τ, while supply is zero. Hence a clearing price must have positive demand and supply; their opposite weak/strict monotonicities imply at most one such price. The computed choices below have strictly slack cash constraints, so the unconstrained formulas do give a clearing solution and establish existence as well. Strict concavity of the underlying problems makes each feasible computed choice globally optimal. The maximum production outlay is nine, below the initial ten. Buyer spending is also at most eighteen, below twenty: in A, writing P=2+Z, spending (P+τ/2)(2P−τ)=2P²−τ²/2≤18; in B it is (P+τ/3)(2P−4τ/3)=2P²−2Pτ/3−4τ²/9≤18. Both cash constraints are slack at the computed choices. The upper bounds on spending and production are (18,9).

Welfare is benefit minus resources, with all transfer recipients included. Ignoring unchanged initial wealth constants, buyer utility is B−pbq, producer profit psq−C, and government revenue τq. Their sum is B−C because pb−ps=τ. Tax receipts cannot also be counted as a new real benefit. Final monetary resources across these accounts equal initial thirty minus the consumed production resources C; the tax merely reallocates money.

Let q0=4+2Z. In A, real welfare is q0q−q²/2=q0²/2−(q−q0)²/2. In B it is (3q0/4)q−3q²/8=3q0²/8−3(q−q0)²/8. These completed squares prove that no-tax q0 is the unique efficient quantity in each maintained model. Substitution of the taxed quantities gives exact real welfare losses τ²/2 in A and 2τ²/3 in B, state by state.

At tax 1, mean quantities are (3,8/3), mean seller prices (3/2,4/3), mean buyer prices (5/2,7/3), mean government receipts (3,8/3), and real welfare losses (1/2,2/3), in A/B order. Even baseline expected real welfare differs: since E[q0²]=20, it is (10,15/2). That value is also not recovered from the observed price/quantity law alone.

What could be learned? A policy pilot assigning tax variation independently of Z can discriminate these two models through quantity slopes −1 and −4/3, if the structural equations, trading rights, population and measurement remain as assumed. Exercise 10 makes a finite-error version precise. This is a statement about discrimination within a declared two-model class. It neither establishes a general identification theorem nor proves that preferences or participation remain invariant under a real tax. Without further evidence, report the different model-dependent counterfactuals rather than select one because its no-tax fit is exact.

7. A complete referee exercise: repair the implementation claim

Worked case 6. The required budget has an infimum but no minimum

Fictional submission. Budget-capped grants uniquely select efficient adoption. “Two agents with adoption costs one and two each receive benefit three when both adopt. A sponsor has one cash unit and promises half to each adopter. Both agents strictly prefer full adoption to unilateral nonadoption at that profile. Therefore the funded policy uniquely implements full adoption, improves everyone’s welfare and proves a subsidy-induced adoption increase. The proof verifies the two full-adoption best replies and invokes finite Nash existence.” These claims are supplied for review, not endorsed.

Complete submitted model. Actions are simultaneous ai∈{0,1}. Utility is ai(baj−ci+si), with (b,c₁,c₂)=(3,1,2). Nonnegative grants are announced before actions and paid on own adoption only. A sponsor with no adoption benefit commits actual cash K and requires s1+s2≤K so every realized obligation is fundable. Each agent can pay its own action cost. The reported policy is (K,s₁,s₂)=(1,1/2,1/2). The solution concept is all independent mixed Nash equilibria; no learning, refinement or tie-selection behavior is assumed. Real surplus is 6a1a2−a1−2a2, with values 0,−1,−2,3 at (0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1). Thus full adoption is uniquely efficient, independently of whether the policy implements it.

Every equilibrium and its account. At the reported grant, adoption gains are 3p2−1/2 and 3p1−3/2. Both pure coordination profiles are equilibria. An equilibrium with a pure player must be one of these, because the opponent’s strict reply forces the same pure profile. If both players mix, the two gain equations give (1/2,1/6). These three profiles exhaust the equilibrium set. With zero grants at the same costs, the same argument gives (0,0),(1,1), and (2/3,1/3).

At full adoption with the fair grant, agents obtain (5/2,3/2), the sponsor loses one and real surplus is 3. At the interior mixture each agent has expected utility zero, while sponsor spending and real welfare are (1/3,−1/3). At no adoption all changes are zero. The sponsor is worse off at full adoption, so the policy is not a Pareto improvement when it is included. Real welfare rises from no adoption to full adoption, but does not rise if both the no-grant and grant games select full adoption. Nor does the model require the policy to select that favorable outcome.

Sharp implementation theorem. More generally let 0<c1,c2<b and s1,s2≥0. Full adoption is the unique Nash equilibrium, including all mixed profiles, if and only if some si>ci.

Necessity. If both si≤ci, each agent weakly prefers nonadoption when the other does not adopt. Thus (0,0) is a Nash equilibrium, even at equality. Full adoption is also an equilibrium because b−ci+si>0. Hence uniqueness fails. Sufficiency. If si>ci, then i’s adoption gain is strictly positive for every opponent probability, so i must adopt with certainty in every equilibrium. The other then strictly adopts because b−cj+sj>0. This forces full adoption and proves uniqueness among all mixed profiles. This is a global incentive argument, not an enumeration of a few grants.

For the original costs, a uniquely implementing grant is feasible if and only if K>1. Necessity follows because at least one grant must strictly exceed its cost and the cheaper cost is one. For any K>1 choose s1=1+δ≤K, s2=0 with δ>0; the grant is actually funded and the theorem applies. The infimum required budget is one, but no budget-minimizing uniquely implementing grant attains it. Supporting full adoption as one equilibrium requires no grant at all. That is a different implementation objective.

The equality boundary is not harmless. At K=1 and grant (1,0), gains become 3p2 and 3p1−2. If p2>0, player 1 must play one, then player 2 must play one. If p2=0, player 1 is indifferent; player 2 is best replying exactly when p1≤2/3. Therefore the complete equilibrium set is

{(p1,0):0≤p1≤2/3} ∪ {(1,1)}.

Assuming that an indifferent player always adopts would change the behavior/selection rule. It is a possible model modification, not a consequence of weak Nash inequalities.

A feasible, bounded extension. Suppose costs are not known precisely: c1∈[3/4,5/4], c2∈[7/4,9/4], while b=3. These are stipulated bounds, not estimated confidence sets. A fixed grant must uniquely implement full adoption for every cost pair in this rectangle. At its upper-cost corner, the necessity argument requires s1>5/4 or s2>9/4. Either inequality is also sufficient throughout the rectangle: it makes that player strictly dominant and b exceeds the other’s largest cost. The robust budget infimum is 5/4, again unattained. Cash K=3/2 and the grant (11/8,0) satisfy the strict requirement. Full-adoption real welfare then lies in [5/2,7/2]. This extension adds a precise uncertainty question and solves it; it does not demand robustness to every conceivable institution.

Benchmark report—summary. The submission studies whether a cash-limited sponsor can select efficient coordination using adoption-contingent grants. This is a meaningful distinction from merely exhibiting an efficient equilibrium. The model’s full-adoption profile is indeed efficient, and the stated fair grant is fundable. However, the argument establishes only that full adoption remains an equilibrium; it does not establish the claimed unique implementation, Pareto improvement or adoption response.

Major issue 1: the best-reply quantifier is wrong. Checking a player’s strict reply when the other adopts compares one opponent profile. Unique implementation requires excluding every other equilibrium profile. Under the submitted grant, no adoption and the independent mixture (1/2,1/6) are additional equilibria. The support calculations above establish both counterexamples and exhaust the set. Finite Nash existence cannot remove them or supply convergence. A revised theorem should explicitly state whether it concerns support of one equilibrium, uniqueness over all equilibria, or a separate selection process.

Major issue 2: the sharp funding boundary is strict. The necessary-and-sufficient condition is that some grant strictly exceed its recipient’s standalone cost. Under these costs, K must be strictly above one. The proposed boundary grant (1,0) still leaves an entire segment of equilibria. A valid revision can prove the K>1 theorem and give the funded targeted construction. Alternatively it can study a specified tie-selection institution, but that would be a new primitive with an enforcement or behavioral justification. Calling the infimum an attained minimum conceals the central difficulty.

Major issue 3: the welfare and empirical interpretations exceed the result. At full adoption the sponsor loses one, so the policy does not improve every participant’s welfare. Transfers cancel in real surplus, leaving three; comparison with the no-grant economy still requires a baseline selection. Observed adoption under a policy would not reveal that the model uniquely selected it. A relevant empirical analysis would record the committed grants, actual payments, adoption costs or credible bounds, joint adoption outcomes and the information/timing that could affect selection. It should distinguish a prediction conditional on the maintained game from evidence supporting that game.

Minor clarification and optional extension. State once that pi is i’s own adoption probability; i’s best reply depends on pj. Make the sponsor’s cash commitment and retained unused balance explicit. The rectangular-cost extension gives a focused robustness question with an exact answer and is a useful possible follow-up. Requiring arbitrary networks, every cost distribution and a new learning theorem would be disproportionate unless one of those features is necessary for the paper’s own headline claim.

Assessment. The unique-implementation and sponsor-inclusive Pareto claims are false as written. A mathematically valid revision is available through the qualified theorem, correct boundary language and narrowed interpretation. Whether that revision constitutes a sufficiently important research contribution is a separate expert judgment; this classroom report cannot settle publication fit. A useful response from an author should state the exact amended claim, give the missing proof or counterexample resolution, and identify any changed assumptions. It should not silently replace the model while keeping the original headline.

Method route: Berk, Harvey and Hirshleifer, Preparing a Referee Report, February 17, 2015, pages 2–7, distinguishes consequential objections from optional improvements and emphasizes evidence and proportionate requests. This is dated methodological guidance, not a binding current journal policy. The fictional report and all mathematical judgments above are supplied independently.

8. Transfer exercises and complete solutions

Preserve the stated information, funding and solution concept unless a prompt changes them. A correct calculation without the relevant quantifier or domain is incomplete. The final exercise uses a ten-point research rubric; its determinate equilibrium and resource claims must still be correct.

  1. For the normalized weighted objective in case 1, find the unique allocations at (1/4,3/4,1/14,13/14). Prove the clipped formula on the entire weight interval. Explain why this sensitivity need not be an identified behavioral comparative static.
  2. In a strict two-by-two matching market, proposers A rank X>Y>outside and B rank Y>X>outside. Recipients X rank B>A>outside and Y rank A>B>outside; all pairs are acceptable. Give proposer- and recipient-proposing deferred-acceptance outcomes and enumerate every stable matching, including partial matchings in the search. Cardinal values are A:(X5,Y4), B:(X4,Y5), X:(A1,B100), Y:(A100,B1). Compare the sum over both sides before and after multiplying both proposers’ utilities by 100. Explain what is ordinal and what is additional welfare structure.
  3. Keep the quartic in case 2, but change the feasible interval to [0,3]. List every endpoint/stationary candidate, identify the unique global maximum and its value, and assess the old strict local maximum at one. Must the constrained maximizer have zero derivative?
  4. Prove the bound 2ε+η from case 2 and show sharpness at (ε,η)=(3/4,1/2). Construct a two-point compact domain, a true objective and an approximating objective, and a permitted returned point that incurs exactly that regret. Explain why a stationary point would not meet the required solver hypothesis by itself.
  5. Change both action costs in case 3 to 3/2, keep benefit three and subsidy one half per adopter, and fund a sponsor account of one. Find every equilibrium, mixed adoption probabilities, full-adoption real welfare and mixed expected sponsor loss/real welfare. Compare the interior mixed probability with the no-subsidy game at the same new costs.
  6. In case 3 at subsidy one half, a mediator privately recommends (1,1) with probability 1/4 and (0,0) otherwise. The sponsor retains its funded account one. Verify every correlated-equilibrium obedience constraint. Find expected total agent utility, sponsor loss and real welfare. Would independent randomization with the same marginals be Nash?
  7. Set θ=15/16 in the case-4 map. Find both algebraic roots, the admissible fixed point and the residual/distance certificate for candidate one third. Derive the local parameter derivative and compare it with the uniform sensitivity bound.
  8. At θ=7/4, a report returns x̂=3/5 and claims computed residual at most one hundredth and uniform map error at most one hundredth. Test both claims jointly. If the uniform error bound is valid, find the minimum possible computed residual. Give a distinct map for which this returned point is exactly fixed, with its true error relative to the original map.
  9. Impose tax 1/2 in case 5. For each model find mean quantity, seller price, buyer price, government receipt and exact real welfare loss. Reconcile the transfer account and state which maintained restrictions make the counterfactual comparison meaningful.
  10. A balanced case-5 pilot at τ=1 has equal numbers of the two Z states. Its measured average quantity differs from the exact model mean by at most ε≥0, with this deterministic bound justified externally. When are the two model prediction intervals disjoint? Analyze ε=1/6. Would successful discrimination identify the economy among all possible models?
  11. In case 6 with costs (1,2), benefit three and budget 3/2, compare unrestricted targeted grants with the additional constraint s1=s2=s. Give a funded uniquely implementing targeted choice. Prove the equal-grant budget infimum and assess attainment. Evaluate equal grants s=3/4, including all equilibria and mixed real welfare.
  12. Referee a fresh claim with benefit four, costs (3/2,5/2), sponsor cash 3/2 and grants (3/4,3/4). The submission claims unique full adoption and a Pareto improvement. Give exact counterexamples and accounts, a sharp budget repair, and a proportionate extension or evidence request. Distinguish major correctness issues from optional suggestions, using the ten-point rubric below.
Solutions, proofs and referee assessment criteria

  1. The four allocations are ((5/2,19/2),(19/2,5/2),(0,12),(12,0)), respectively. The derivative’s denominator is positive and its numerator is 14λ−1−x. It is positive to the left of that root and negative to the right. If the root is below zero, the objective decreases over the feasible interval and selects zero; if above twelve, it increases and selects twelve. At the two exact boundary roots, all interior points are strictly worse than the endpoint. At λ=0 or1, strict monotonicity proves the same endpoint conclusion. Thus the clipped formula is global and unique. Changing λ changes the social objective while preserving individual rankings and feasible choices. Without an additional normative or money-metric assumption, those choices do not identify λ.

  2. There are 7 feasible matchings: empty, four single-pair matchings and two perfect matchings. The first five have an unmatched proposer and an unmatched recipient who find each other acceptable; that pair blocks. In M1=(AX,BY), each proposer gets its first choice, so no unmatched pair can be preferred by both sides. In M2=(AY,BX), every recipient gets its first choice, also preventing blocking. These are exactly the two stable matchings. Proposer DA stops immediately at M1; recipient DA stops immediately at M2, because their distinct first-choice proposals are all accepted.

    Total assigned values in (M1,M2) are (12,208). After the proposers’ positive rescaling, they are (1002,1000). Each individual ranking and every blocking comparison is unchanged, but the preferred sum reverses. Stability and these DA outcomes are ordinal facts. Choosing an interpersonal cardinal sum is additional structure; no assertion about all matching institutions, ties, capacity, transfers or group incentives follows from this enumeration.

  3. The candidates are zero, one, two and three, with values (0,37,32,45). Four is infeasible. The derivative is positive from two to three, so the unique global maximizer is the constrained endpoint three, with value forty-five. The local maximum at one now has regret 8. At the global endpoint, the derivative is 24, not zero; moving farther right would improve the objective but is not feasible. This is a genuinely changed constraint set, not a validation of the original local-only argument.

  4. For a true maximizer x*, add and subtract f̂ at x* and the returned x̂. The two function-approximation terms are each at most ε, while the intervening approximate-objective gap is at most η by the global certificate. This proves 2ε+η without assuming f̂ attains its supremum. For sharpness, take the compact two-point set {A,B}, values f(A)=0, f(B)=2, f̂(A)=3/4, f̂(B)=5/4, and return A. The largest absolute error is three quarters and the approximate gap is one half, while true regret is 2. It exactly equals 2ε+η. A zero gradient on another problem says nothing about its global approximate-objective gap; case 2’s strict local maximum is a counterexample.

  5. The adoption gain is 3pj−1. The pure coordination profiles remain equilibria, and any equilibrium with a pure player must be one of those. If both mix, both gains vanish, so the unique interior profile is (1/3,1/3). With no subsidy and the same costs, its probabilities are (1/2,1/2). Full adoption yields each agent utility two, sponsor loss one and real welfare 3. At the subsidized mixture, expected agent utilities are zero, sponsor spending is one third, and real welfare is −1/3. The funded account covers both simultaneous grants in the full-adoption event. A fall on this interior branch is not an empirical selection prediction.

  6. Both recommendations have positive probability. Conditional on recommendation one, the other agent certainly adopts; obeying gives 5/2 rather than zero. Conditional on recommendation zero, the other does not adopt; deviating gives −1/2 rather than zero. These are every nontrivial binary recommendation-contingent deviation, so the joint law is a CE. Expected total agent utility, sponsor loss and real welfare are (5/4,1/4,1). No event requires more than the already funded one unit.

    With independent adoption probabilities one quarter instead, an agent’s adoption gain is 1/4, strictly positive. Mixing is therefore not optimal and the independent profile is not Nash. Equal unconditional marginals do not preserve the conditional information created by a mediator. This comparison changes the joint recommendation law and deviation rights; it does not demonstrate that an unmodeled institution will implement the correlated law.

  7. The roots are (1/4,15/4); only one quarter belongs to the invariant interval. At candidate one third the residual is 1/3−(15/16+1/9)/4=41/576. The certified distance is 41/288, while actual distance is 1/12. The explicit-root derivative is 1/(4−2x*)=2/7. This is local to the specified parameter; the one-half Lipschitz constant covers the entire parameter interval and does not assume the same local slope everywhere.

  8. The two claimed errors would bound true residual by 1/50, but it is 29/400. They would also bound distance by one twenty-fifth, whereas it is one tenth. At least one claimed bound fails. If the uniform map error is at most one hundredth, the triangle inequality requires computed residual at least 1/16. This minimum is attained: T̂(x)=T7/4(x)+1/100 has uniform error exactly 1/100, image [179/400,279/400] inside [0,1], and residual |3/5−T̂(3/5)|=1/16. The alternative T51/25 fixes three fifths exactly, but its uniform difference from T7/4 is 29/400. Setting numerical residual zero and that valid map error gives distance bound 29/200. The bounds diagnose a model/numerical distinction; they do not prove that the alternative map is a better economic model.

  9. In requested order—mean quantity, seller price, buyer price, government receipt, real loss—the A results are (7/2,7/4,9/4,7/4,1/8), and the B results are (10/3,5/3,13/6,5/3,1/6). Substitute τ=1/2 in the solved statewise expressions and average Z; the loss formulas do not depend on Z. Buyer spending includes τq, seller receipts exclude it, and government receives it, so summing utilities/profits leaves B−C. The comparison maintains each structural demand/cost equation, price-taking behavior, the exogenous intervention, information, enforcement, population and the verified slack cash constraints. Observational fit by itself establishes none of that policy invariance.

  10. The prediction intervals are [3−ε,3+ε] and [8/3−ε,8/3+ε]. Their centers differ by one third. They are disjoint exactly when ε<1/6; equality is not enough. At ε=1/6 they touch at 17/6, which is consistent with both models. A measured mean outside one interval can reject that model under the maintained deterministic bound and invariance assumptions. It does not establish identification among every conceivable model, validate the bound itself or show that another admissible structural model would make the same policy prediction. Exact balance removes the known state-composition difference; it is not a general statistical confidence argument.

  11. A target grant (5/4,0) is feasible under cash 3/2. Agent 1 then strictly adopts against every opponent action; agent 2 strictly follows. Full-adoption agent utilities, sponsor loss and real surplus are ((13/4,1),5/4,3). Under the equal-grant restriction, unique full adoption requires s>1: by the proved theorem, s must strictly exceed at least one cost, and the smaller cost is one. The total budget must therefore be strictly above two; its infimum 2 is unattained. Cash 3/2 allows only s≤3/4 and cannot accomplish unique implementation with equal grants.

    At s=3/4, the full Nash set is the two pure coordination profiles and the interior mixture (5/12,1/12). Both grant-adjusted costs remain strictly between zero and the benefit, so the same support proof is complete. Each mixing agent has zero expected utility, expected sponsor spending is three eighths, and real welfare is −3/8. The equity-of-grants restriction changes the feasible policy set and the funding requirement; it is not a numerical error in the targeted solution.

  12. The fresh model has gains 4p2−3/4 and 4p1−7/4. Both pure coordination profiles are equilibria; the complete support argument gives the additional interior mixture (7/16,3/16). Expected agent utilities there are zero, sponsor expected loss is 15/32, and real welfare is −15/32. At full adoption agent utilities are (13/4,9/4), sponsor loss is 3/2 and real surplus is 4. The sponsor therefore does not enjoy a Pareto improvement.

    The generalized theorem applies because both costs are positive and below benefit four. Unique implementation requires s1>3/2 or s2>5/2. Required-budget infimum 3/2 is unattained; any K>3/2 can finance a grant just above 3/2 to agent 1. Checking best replies only at full adoption proves that it is one equilibrium, not that it is the only one. A sound report should give these exact counterexamples, preserve the sponsor’s account, distinguish an additional tie-selection rule from a proof repair, and ask which maintained game/selection facts would be supported by data.

    Ten-point rubric. Award two points for a faithful question/model/quantifier summary; two for the complete equilibrium counterexamples and exact accounts; two for the necessary-and-sufficient strict funding repair and unattained boundary; two for sponsor-inclusive welfare, selection and identification limits; and two for a relevant bounded extension or evidence request with explicit primitives and a clear required-versus-optional distinction. For example, a finite interval of cost uncertainty can be analyzed at its worst-cost corner, provided the benefit still exceeds all possible costs. A report need not advocate the subsidy or a particular journal decision to receive full credit. Unsupported accusations, a request for unlimited robustness, or a mere list of stylistic preferences does not replace the substantive audit.

9. Teach-back, reproduction and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why a correct local calculation, an existing equilibrium, a small computed residual and exact observational fit answer different questions. A complete answer uses the quartic’s twenty-seven-unit local regret; the adoption game’s multiple pure/mixed outcomes; the contraction constant and separate map/numerical errors; and the two equally fitting markets’ different tax slopes. Identify a repair in each case that preserves the original question, and identify a proposed change that instead creates a new model.

Teach-back benchmark. For the quartic, comparing all feasible critical points and endpoints repairs the original global claim; replacing its objective by a concave quadratic changes the model. For adoption, reporting the full equilibrium set preserves the game; adding a selection or learning rule adds an assumption that needs its own justification. For the activity map, a bound on the original residual together with its contraction constant certifies the original computation; solving a different map exactly does not. For the tax question, presenting both model-conditional predictions honestly preserves the available evidence; claiming a single policy effect requires additional invariance restrictions or a new discriminating design, whose credibility must be assessed separately.

Delayed retention. Without consulting the equations, reconstruct the sharp objective-error bound, the binary adoption best-reply threshold, the strict funding condition for unique implementation, and the tax-pilot discrimination boundary. Explain why positive utility rescaling leaves stability comparisons unchanged but can alter a welfare sum. State whether a computed map’s fixed point proves that the original map was solved.

Answer key. Insert the approximate objective twice around a true maximum and returned point to get 2ε+η, with a global solver-gap hypothesis. Adoption is optimal when b times the opponent’s probability exceeds own cost minus grant; equality permits mixing. With both costs below the coordination benefit, unique adoption requires a grant strictly above at least one standalone cost; weak equality retains no adoption and can generate a continuum. Prediction intervals with centers one third apart and radius ε are disjoint only for ε<1/6. Positive rescaling preserves each individual comparison but changes relative interpersonal weights. A fixed point of the computed map is accurate for the original only with a justified map-error and stability bound.

Reproduction. Use exact fractions to enumerate the seven partial matchings and test every potential blocker; factor the polynomial derivative before comparing all feasible critical points/endpoints; solve the binary gain equations together with every pure-support case; and reconstruct the buyer, producer, sponsor and government accounts separately before consolidating. The Python standard library’s fractions.Fraction suffices for every displayed rational result. Editorial checks compare independent primitive calculations, full derivative identities and focused boundary interventions. Neither a bid/action grid nor a solver’s success flag stands in for the universal arguments printed here.

This closes the graduate microeconomic theory sequence by making proof, model choice and interpretation part of the same research discipline. The next volume develops graduate macroeconomics and macro-finance. The habit to carry forward is precise: establish what the model proves, identify what selects or implements its outcomes, and state what evidence could support the economic interpretation.

Sources and further study

  • Simon Board and Moritz Meyer-ter-Vehn, Writing Economic Theory Papers — A stated economic question, transparent model primitives and qualified contribution; separating theorem, proof and interpretation. Used in original C12 critique and writing instruction; not evidence for the new models.
  • Jonathan B. Berk, Campbell R. Harvey and David Hirshleifer, Preparing a Referee Report: Guidelines and Perspectives — A referee’s concise contribution summary, evidence for consequential objections, distinction between required repair and optional extension, and proportionate follow-up. Used in original C12 critique and writing instruction; not evidence for the new models.
  • Muhamet Yildiz, Graduate Game Theory (Cover Spring2022; hosted in the MIT2024 course. Physical page equals printed Arabic page+8 in inspected chapter sections.) — Finite mixed Nash, finite common-prior Bayesian games and positive-type qualification, private recommendation CE and Nash-product relation.
